title: Views Instead of Copies
goal: A slice is a borrowed window into existing data. No allocation, no copy.

sections.text: A slice is a reference to a part of a collection: a pointer and a length. Writing `&data[1..4]` does not copy elements 1, 2, and 3. It creates a view of them, and the original collection stays the owner. The string version of this is `&str`, which is a view into UTF-8 text.

sections.caption: A range makes a view, not a copy.

sections.text: Ranges are half-open: `1..4` includes index 1 and excludes index 4, so the length is always end minus start. Methods like `split` and `trim` follow the same principle. They return subslices of their input instead of new allocations.

A view borrows from its source, so it cannot outlive it. A function can return a slice of its input, and lifetime elision connects the two automatically. A function cannot return a slice of a local variable, because the local is dropped when the function ends. That is error `E0515`, and one puzzle in this deck walks straight into it.
The instinct this deck trains: return a view when the caller just reads, and pay for an owned copy with `.to_vec()` or `.to_owned()` only when the caller must keep the data alive on its own.

explanation: A slice is a pointer plus a length into existing data. Prefer views for reading; pay for a copy only when the caller must own the result.
